verdicts.note: publishersweekly.com/9780553103540 fetched raw (HTTP 200, browser UA). Review body: 'Although conventional in form, the book stands out from similar work by Eddings, Brooks and others by virtue of its superbly developed characters, accomplished prose and sheer bloody-mindedness.' Page metadata 'Reviewed on: 07/29/1996' confirms the 29 July 1996 date; a sidebar entry confirms PW starred it. Quote exact; every limb supported.

paullevinson.blogspot.com post fetched raw (HTTP 200). Header on the post: 'from Tangent Magazine, #16, Fall 1996 ... Reviewed by Paul Levinson'; body: 'Martin writes as convincingly of tart juices oozing from an apple as of sleet on the side of a mountain'. Quote exact; 'sleet on a mountainside' is the page's 'sleet on the side of a mountain'. Levinson notes in the comments that the URL's '2006' is his own typo and the review is 1996.
Same page, same sentence's continuation: 'and his book is as much an adventure of the senses as it is of the mind.' Quote exact; claim fully supported.
Same page, paragraph 2: 'The settings are equally diverse and evocative.' Quote exact as a full sentence; claim fully supported.

Same page, paragraph beginning 'But the dragon thread has other problems.': 'The descriptive passages are marvelous - you can smell the spice, and taste it in every cup of wine Martin renders'. Quote exact. The review never uses the name Daenerys: it calls this 'the dragon thread' and identifies it as the 'Blood of the Dragon' novella following the pretender's sister, given as bride to a 'Ghenghis Khan-type character' — i.e. unambiguously the Daenerys thread, so the claim's label is a naming of what the page describes, not an added assertion.

Same page, supernatural paragraph: 'But the actual brief appearance of these cold nightmares-come-true has far less impact than their suggestion.' Quote exact; the 'cold creatures' limb is the page's 'cold, slouching beast[s]' / 'cold nightmares-come-true'.

Same page, next sentence: 'Similarly, the dragons work better as natural history - they're believed to have died out over a century before the action begins in this book, and their skeletons are admired, feared, and lamented by various characters who contemplate them - than as actual hatchlings at the end of the novel.' Quote exact; every limb (natural history, skeletons admired/feared/lamented by characters, versus living hatchlings) is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: episodic feel 'underlined by' the chapter alternation, not caused by it
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the causal attribution: the review attributes the growing episodic quality to the threads developing independently and says the POV alternation 'underlines' it, rather than attributing the episodic feel to the alternation
verdicts.note: fanac.org/fanzines/Vector/Vector192.pdf fetched raw (HTTP 200, 10.99 MB) and text extracted with pypdf; page index 18 carries the running head 'Vector 192 - March/April 1997' and the folio 'page 19', with 'George R.R. Martin / Reviewed by Steve Jeffery / A Game of Thrones'. Full sentence: '...threads start to develop independently towards the end, things become more episodic, underlined by Martin's technique of alternating chapters between a number of major viewpoint characters.' Quote exact; date, reviewer, venue and page all confirmed. Only the causal connective overstates the source.

Same PDF page: 'A Game of Thrones appears with all the distinguishing features of the fantasy blockbuster, as Book One of A Song of Fire and Ice. Those distinguishing features include a map, cunningly divided into The North and The South, an Appendix listing a cast of Cecil B. DeMille proportions, and the obligatory jacket blurb...'. Quote exact; the appendix cast list is explicitly one of the listed 'distinguishing features of the fantasy blockbuster'.

Same PDF page: the blurb quoted by Jeffery announces 'the most imaginative, ambitious and compelling fantasy epic since Lord of the Rings' and Martin as yet another 'true heir' to Tolkien; the next paragraph opens 'This sort of gushing hype does no favours to anybody, least of all Martin.' and the paragraph closes 'A Game of Thrones deserves better.' Quote exact (including the trailing comma); the 'no favours to the book' limb is carried by 'deserves better'.

publishersweekly.com/9780553801477 fetched raw (HTTP 200). First sentence: 'A few images recur in the enormously complex fifth installment of Martin's massively multicharacter epic: the chess-like game cyvasse, small rivers flowing into larger ones, ships and armies battered by terrible storms.' Quote exact; all three images and the 2011 date ('Reviewed on: 05/30/2011') confirmed.

kirkusreviews.com raw page fetched (HTTP 200, browser UA). Paragraph 2: 'There's the usual blend of exposition, sometimes seemingly endless, and the usual swords-and-sorcery dialogue:' followed by exactly three quoted lines ('The plunder from Astapor...', 'Two kings to wake the dragon...', 'False friends, treacherous servants...'). 'Review Posted Online: Sept. 26, 2011' confirms the date. Quote exact; the three-lines limb confirmed by count.
Same Kirkus page, same sentence: 'There's the usual blend of exposition, sometimes seemingly endless'. Quote exact; claim fully supported.

Same Kirkus page: 'Martin has been likened to J.R.R. Tolkien, but Tolkien was never quite so ponderous, and certainly not so obsessed with bodily functions of various sorts'. Quote exact; the comparison's implied second term is Martin, named in the same sentence.

Same Kirkus sentence continues '...and certainly not so obsessed with bodily functions of various sorts:' followed by exactly two quoted lines ('The Grand Maester befouled himself in dying...' and 'When you bugger a man you expect a squeal or two.'), then 'Indeed.' Quote exact; the charge lands on Martin by the Tolkien contrast, and the two-lines limb is confirmed by count.
